questions.question: In a distributed lag model $Y_t = \alpha + \beta_0 X_t + \beta_1 X_{t-1} + \dots + u_t$ where lag weights decay geometrically ($\beta_k = \beta_0 \lambda^k$ with $0 < \lambda < 1$), applying the Koyck transformation produces $Y_t = \alpha(1-\lambda) + \lambda Y_{t-1} + \beta_0 X_t + v_t$. What is the primary econometric problem created by this transformation?
options: The composite error term becomes $v_t = u_t - \lambda u_{t-1}$, which is correlated with the regressor $Y_{t-1}$, rendering OLS inconsistent.
The error term $v_t$ exhibits pure heteroskedasticity proportional to $X_t$, rendering OLS biased but consistent.
The transformation induces exact multicollinearity between $Y_{t-1}$ and $X_t$, making OLS non-estimable.
The error term $v_t$ becomes completely deterministic, violating the zero conditional mean assumption.

questions.question: When nonparametrically estimating a conditional expectation $E[Y|X=x]$, how does local linear regression compare to the standard Nadaraya-Watson (local constant) kernel estimator near the boundaries of the support of $X$?
options: Local linear regression exhibits boundary bias of order $O(h)$, whereas Nadaraya-Watson achieves $O(h^2)$ bias automatically.
Both estimators suffer equally from $O(h)$ boundary bias, but local linear regression has lower asymptotic variance.
Nadaraya-Watson exhibits $O(h)$ boundary bias, whereas local linear regression automatically adapts at boundaries to maintain $O(h^2)$ bias.
Local linear regression requires the bandwidth $h \to \infty$ near boundaries, converting it into a global linear model.

questions.question: Suppose the true data generating process is $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + u$, where $E[u|X_1, X_2] = 0$. If an researcher omits $X_2$ and estimates $Y = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 X_1 + e$ via OLS, what is the probability limit of the estimator $\hat{\alpha}_1$?
options: \text{plim } \hat{\alpha}_1 = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \frac{\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)}{\text{Var}(X_2)}
\text{plim } \hat{\alpha}_1 = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \frac{\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)}{\text{Var}(X_1)}
\text{plim } \hat{\alpha}_1 = \beta_1 - \beta_2 \frac{\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)}{\text{Var}(X_1)}
\text{plim } \hat{\alpha}_1 = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)}{\text{Var}(X_1)} + \beta_2

questions.question: In Instrumental Variables (IV) / Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation with $L$ instruments and $K$ endogenous regressors ($L > K$), what is the null hypothesis ($H_0$) and asymptotic distribution of Hansen's $J$-statistic?
options: $H_0$: All $L$ instruments are invalid; $J \sim \chi^2(L + K)$
$H_0$: At least one instrument is valid; $J \sim \chi^2(K)$
$H_0$: All $L$ moment conditions are valid (instruments are exogenous); $J \sim \chi^2(L - K)$
$H_0$: The endogenous regressors are actually exogenous; $J \sim F(L-K, N-L)$
